statement: Exposure plays no part. The cued base's short, low-entropy right answers are ordinary sampling from a high-entropy model on easy problems, not reproduced solutions: a fresh sample of the same problem often comes out at a very different length. The RL-minus-cued-base gap tracks difficulty and termination, and the +6.9-point post-cutoff excess is single-sample noise on about 60 post problems.
why_strongest: Test 1 (+6.9) is about 1.1 sd from zero, using the theory's own interval [-3, 17] for one sample per model on about 60 post problems, so the excess needs no exposure term. Test 2 came out with the opposite sign to the recall prediction (+0.14 against -0.3): on pre-cutoff problems the base's both-right answers are not shorter relative to RL's. Test 3 (0.845) is the generic confidence-length pattern: short answers belong to easy problems, and long answers carry more branching tokens (2505.17813, 2506.01939). The board shows the gap growing with length in every quartile and coming from cap hits and failure to finish (knowledge-9e4147, result-5de032, knowledge-1497e8). Code-RL closes the MATH-500 gap with no math reward (result-4b0d5f). A fresh base sample solves 40 of the 65 'RL-only' problems (result-9b6af3), which is sampling variance, not missing procedures. Olmo-3's contamination flags do not track corpus exposure (2611.10307). The advocate defends the theory by saying the year-split tests are too noisy to decide, so these replacement tests move to MATH-500, where n is large. Recall has a consequence there that the advocate cannot wave away as noise: a recalled solution is a fixed text, so on recalled (short) problems the base should give nearly the same length on every sample, more consistently than RL's search-style procedure. Under this rival the base at T 1.0 / top-p 1.0 is the higher-entropy, mode-mixing model: its right answers have median 1,432 but mean 3,933 tokens, against RL's 3,014 and 4,694. So the base's lengths vary across samples at least as much as RL's, and most of all on short problems.

tests.experiment: MATH-500, 4 independent samples per model at T 1.0: on problems that both models solve every time and where the base's typical answer is short, how much the base's answer length varies across its own samples, relative to how much RL's varies (median log ratio of coefficients of variation).
tests.recipe: Files: studies/rlneurons/results/day1_3/math500_base_cue-01/rows.jsonl (base) and studies/rlneurons/results/day1_3/math500_rl-01/rows.jsonl (RL). Use only rows with attempt == 0. For each model and problem_index, collect the attempt-0 rows for samples 0, 1, 2 and 3. Keep a problem only if both models have all four attempt-0 rows, and every one of those 8 rows has score_v3 == 1 and cap_hit false. Missing rows exclude the problem; there are no ties to break. For each kept problem and model, take the 4 values of n_new, and set CV = (population standard deviation, ddof = 0) / (mean). Drop any problem where either model's CV is 0. Short problems are those where the median of the base's 4 n_new values (the mean of the two middle values) is <= 2000. For each short problem, compute L = ln(CV_base / CV_RL). Statistic = median of L over short problems (for an even count, the mean of the two middle values).
tests.theory_should_say: The theory says short base right answers are recalled pretraining solutions and RL's are learned procedures. A recalled text comes back at nearly the same length every time, so on these problems the base's CV should sit below RL's, a clearly negative log ratio of about -0.2 to -0.3. Here the base is the noisier, mode-mixing sampler, so its CV is at or above RL's.

tests.experiment: MATH-500, same 4-sample rows: base-versus-RL length variability on short problems minus the same on long problems (difference in median log CV ratios).
tests.recipe: Same files, attempt-0 rows, kept problems (all 8 rows score_v3 == 1 and cap_hit false), CV definition, zero-CV drops and L = ln(CV_base / CV_RL) as in the first test here. Short = median of the base's 4 n_new values <= 2000; long = that median > 2000. Statistic = (median L over short problems) - (median L over long problems), with each median taken as in the first test (for an even count, the mean of the two middle values).
tests.theory_should_say: Recall applies only on the short (recalled) problems, so the theory makes the base unusually consistent there and not on long, procedural problems. That gives a negative difference of about -0.3. Here there is no recall, so the difference is near zero, or slightly positive because the 16,384 cap compresses the length spread of long base answers.
